opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think this is one of the most important things to keep track of, and also one of the hardest. The core worry is that once AI systems are meaningfully speeding up AI research itself, you can get a feedback loop where progress compounds faster than our institutions, or even the companies themselves, can notice and react. So I'd want monitoring on a few different levels.

The first is capability evaluations that directly target AI R&D. Not just "can the model solve hard coding puzzles," but "can it do the actual tasks that research engineers at frontier labs do day to day?" Can it run an experiment end to end, debug a training run, write and optimize kernels, propose and test a research idea? There's been good work building benchmarks like that, and I think we want them to get more realistic and longer-horizon, because the gap between a two-hour task and a two-week project is where a lot of the uncertainty lives.

But benchmarks only tell you about potential. The second level, which I think is actually more important and much more neglected, is measuring real-world uplift inside the labs. How much of the code being merged is AI-written? How much compute is being directed by AI agents rather than humans? If you gave researchers access to the internal model versus withholding it, how much faster do they get things done? You can run that kind of controlled study. And you'd want to track trends over time, because what matters isn't any single number but whether the curve is bending.

The third level is something like early warning indicators at the level of the whole field. Things like: is the rate of algorithmic progress speeding up? Are labs starting to say they're bottlenecked on compute rather than on researcher time? That shift would tell you a lot, because it suggests that human labor is no longer the binding constraint.

The tricky part is that almost all of this information sits inside a handful of companies, and they have competitive reasons not to share it. So I'm pretty excited about some form of transparency requirement, where labs have to report on internal AI usage for R&D, maybe to a government body or a trusted third party, even if it isn't made fully public. Because the scenario I worry about is one where the intelligence explosion, or whatever you want to call it, is mostly happening inside a lab's internal deployment, and the outside world only finds out when a much more capable model gets released, or doesn't get released at all.

And I'd add that we should decide in advance what we'd do with the information. It's not that useful to monitor if there isn't some agreed-upon threshold where, say, AI is doing most of the research labor, at which point labs commit to more safety measures, slower scaling, or more external oversight. Otherwise you just get a really well-documented history of how we lost the ability to steer.

r001.rationale: The response recommends tracking AI research tasks, lab usage, compute direction, and field-level progress, but does not cover the entire production stack or hardware manufacturing.

r002.rationale: It describes a feedback loop when AI meaningfully speeds up research, but does not identify full automation of AI production as roughly coinciding with expected dramatic acceleration.

r003.rationale: The response does not recommend studying early AI power users outside AI production.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something I've been thinking about a lot, because I think the most important question for how the next several years go is basically: how much does AI speed up AI R&D itself? And right now I think we're flying somewhat blind on that.

The way I'd frame it is there's a few different things you could try to measure, and they have different tradeoffs. The simplest and most legible thing is uplift studies. You take a bunch of researchers at a lab, you randomize who gets access to the latest models and who doesn't, or who gets the frontier model versus a weaker one, and you measure how fast they complete tasks. METR has done versions of this. The problem is that those studies are expensive, they're slow, and they measure the wrong population in some sense. Most of the acceleration that matters is going to happen inside frontier labs, on frontier-lab-specific workflows, and those people are not going to volunteer to be in the control arm for six months. There's also a real selection issue where the people who are most enthusiastic about using AI tools are probably also the people who've figured out how to get the most out of them, and a short study doesn't capture the learning curve.

So the second thing, which I think is more promising but harder to do well, is just asking the labs to report. What fraction of code that gets merged into your training stack was written primarily by a model? What fraction of your researchers say they would be, you know, less than half as productive without these tools? How many experiments are being proposed, run, and interpreted end to end by an agent with a human just signing off? I'd want those numbers published, ideally by every frontier developer, on some regular cadence, with enough methodological detail that you can tell whether the number means anything. Right now you get these anecdotal claims, somebody says ninety percent of our code is written by AI, and that's nearly meaningless without knowing what counts as code, what counts as written by, and whether it's boilerplate or the hard stuff.

The third thing, and this is the one I'm actually most worried about, is that I think the thing we most care about isn't the current speedup, it's the second derivative. Like, if AI is currently making AI research twenty percent faster, that's fine, that's just a normal productivity tool. If it's making it twenty percent faster this year and it's going to be fifty percent next year and three hundred percent the year after, that's a totally different world, and the gap between those worlds is not very visible from the inside. People's intuitions are anchored on what the tools can do today. So I'd want monitoring that specifically tries to extrapolate. Track the trend in how long a task a model can do autonomously before it falls over. Track how much human oversight per unit of research output is needed and whether that's dropping. And have some pre-committed thresholds where, if the trend crosses them, that triggers something, whether that's a disclosure requirement, or some external review, or just a serious conversation about slowing down.

The honest thing to say is I don't think any of this is going to be perfectly reliable. The labs have incentives to understate it to avoid regulation and also incentives to overstate it for marketing, and those pull in different directions depending on the audience. But I'd much rather have imperfect, somewhat gameable numbers that are at least publicly reported and argued over than the current situation, where the people who actually know are inside the labs and everyone else is guessing from Twitter demos.

r001.rationale: The response focuses on AI R&D workflows at frontier labs, such as coding, experiments, and researcher productivity. It does not recommend monitoring the entire production stack or mention hardware manufacturing.

r002.rationale: It discusses increasing AI-driven research speed and tracking trends, but does not identify full automation of AI production or connect it to futurists’ expectations of a dramatic acceleration in progress.

r003.rationale: It notes that AI power users may get more out of tools, but only in the context of selection bias in research studies. It does not recommend studying power users outside AI production for transferable insights.

astra-6.text:
I think the key thing to track is how much AI is speeding up the actual work of AI research and development. It’s not enough to ask, “How good is this model at coding?” You want to know whether a research team using it can get to a given improvement in capability faster, with fewer people, or with less compute.

That means looking at the whole process: coming up with ideas, implementing experiments, interpreting the results, and deciding what to try next. A system could be extremely helpful at writing code but still have a fairly modest effect overall if humans are doing all the work of choosing promising experiments.

Ideally, you’d have evaluations where models work on research projects that take people days or weeks, alongside evidence from how researchers are actually using them. How much can you delegate? How often does a person need to intervene? And are the models producing improvements that actually make it into the next generation of systems?

The thing I’d be particularly interested in is whether that feedback loop is getting stronger: better AI makes research faster, which produces better AI, which makes research faster again. We shouldn’t assume that automatically implies an explosive acceleration—there could be substantial bottlenecks. But we should be measuring those bottlenecks and how quickly they’re disappearing.

r001.rationale: It recommends tracking AI’s effect across AI research and development, but does not include hardware manufacturing in the production stack.

r002.rationale: It discusses a stronger feedback loop and cautions against assuming explosive acceleration, but does not identify full automation as coinciding with futurists’ expected acceleration point.

r003.rationale: It recommends evidence from researchers’ use of AI, but does not discuss early AI power users outside AI production or how their experience could transfer.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the thing we most want to track is how much AI is accelerating AI research and development in practice. It’s tempting to focus on whether a model can solve a particular coding problem or answer questions about machine learning, but there’s a big gap between doing well on those tasks and making the whole research process substantially faster.

So I’d want to look at actual workflows inside AI companies. What fraction of researchers’ work can these systems do? How much supervision do they need? Can they run experiments, interpret the results, and decide what to try next? And, ultimately, does a team with access to these systems make more progress than a comparable team without them?

One important distinction is between speeding up an individual task and speeding up the entire process. If writing code gets ten times faster, but you’re still waiting on experiments or struggling to decide which experiments are worth running, the overall acceleration could be much smaller. You need to understand those bottlenecks and how they’re changing.

I’d also want to monitor this before systems can do research fully autonomously. You could get a substantial acceleration from systems that are useful assistants to lots of researchers. The question isn’t just, ‘Have we built an automated AI researcher yet?’ It’s, ‘How much faster is the feedback loop getting, and how quickly is that acceleration itself increasing?’

r001.rationale: The response focuses on AI research workflows inside AI companies and does not recommend monitoring the full production stack, including hardware manufacturing and software development.

r002.rationale: It says meaningful acceleration can occur before fully autonomous research, but does not connect full automation of AI production to futurists’ expected point of dramatic progress acceleration.

r003.rationale: It does not recommend studying early AI power users outside AI production.
